chunks.title: Chemical burn: first 15 minutes
chunks.tldr: Irrigate BEFORE checking vision (unless open globe suspected). Saline/Ringer's — tap water is fine and may beat saline for alkali. Never neutralise acid with alkali. Speculum + anaesthetic, evert both lids, sweep fornices. Wait 5–10 min, check pH; continue till 7.0–7.4 (may need >10 L).
points: Alkali: lye, cement, plaster, airbag powder, bleach, ammonia. Acids: battery acid, pool cleaner.
IV tubing on a saline bag = easiest irrigation.
Read litmus before it dries.
Persistently abnormal pH → hunt for retained particles: double eversion with Desmarres retractor.
Embedded acid/alkali particles may need surgical removal.
History: what chemical, when, how long before irrigation, eye protection; bring the label/MSDS.
chunks.hook: Water first, questions later.

cards.q: Target pH before stopping irrigation?
cards.a: 7.0–7.4 (check 5–10 min after pausing).

cards.q: Why never neutralise an alkali burn with acid?
cards.a: The acid–base reaction can generate heat and harmful products (secondary thermal injury).

chunks.title: Chemical burn: mild vs severe treatment
chunks.tldr: Mild–moderate (no limbal blanching): cycloplegic, PF tears/antibiotic ointment, ± steroid + antibiotic for a week, pain relief, treat IOP (avoid alpha-agonists). Severe (blanching, opaque cornea): admit, debride, cycloplegic (no phenylephrine), antibiotic + steroid, doxycycline + vit C, sweep fornices, amniotic membrane/ProKera.
points: Epithelium totally gone → only Bowman left, which stains poorly; re-apply fluorescein.
IOP: acetazolamide/methazolamide (watch K⁺), add timolol. Avoid alpha-agonists (vasoconstrict).
Steroids: taper by 7–14 days (melt risk); longer anti-inflammatory → medroxyprogesterone 1%.
Ciprofloxacin can precipitate in big defects.
Ascorbate/citrate speed alkali healing (caution in renal disease).
Melting: acetylcysteine; perforation: cyanoacrylate glue, patch graft; keratoplasty better after 12–18 months.
Late: tarsorrhaphy, limbal stem cell transplant from fellow eye.
Super glue: separate lids gently, trim lashes, warm saline/ointment, treat defects as abrasions.
chunks.hook: Blanched limbus = bad burn. Steroids out by 2 weeks.

cards.q: Which dilating drop should be avoided in chemical burns with limbal ischaemia?
cards.a: Phenylephrine (vasoconstrictor).

cards.q: Oral agents that reduce collagenolysis after a severe burn?
cards.a: Doxycycline 100 mg b.i.d. and vitamin C.

chunks.title: Corneal abrasion
chunks.tldr: Staining defect with no infiltrate. Evert lids (vertical lines → subtarsal FB). Non-CL wearer: antibiotic ointment/drops. Contact lens wearer → antipseudomonal (fluoroquinolone), never patch. Fingernail/vegetable → fluoroquinolone. Never give topical anaesthetic to take home.
points: DDx: recurrent erosion, HSV, confluent SPK, UV, exposure, neurotrophic, chemical.
Cycloplegic for traumatic iritis (24–72 h later); avoid steroids while epithelium open.
Patching rarely needed; never in CL-related abrasions.
Short NSAID drop course (ketorolac × 3 days) for pain.
Debride loose epithelium.
Bandage CL only with antibiotic cover and close follow-up; not for CL-related or infected.
Follow-up: big/central next day; small/peripheral 2–5 days.
CL wearer: resume a week after eye feels normal, with a new lens.
chunks.hook: Contact lens + abrasion = Pseudomonas risk → quinolone, no patch.

cards.q: Antibiotic choice for an abrasion in a contact lens wearer?
cards.a: A fluoroquinolone (antipseudomonal); no patching.

cards.q: Why not prescribe topical anaesthetic drops?
cards.a: They delay epithelial healing and raise infection/ulcer risk.

chunks.title: Foreign bodies & conjunctival laceration
chunks.tldr: Always ask: metal on metal? hammering? power tools? → think IOFB. Dilate, consider CT (not MRI). Remove corneal FB with spud/needle at slit lamp; burr the rust ring (deep central ring can wait). Treat defect like an abrasion (not erythromycin alone). Conjunctival lac: explore the sclera underneath; most heal, suture if ≥1–1.5 cm.
points: Small reactive sterile infiltrate around FB is common; big AC reaction/discharge → culture, treat as keratitis.
Look for entry wounds, iris holes/TIDs, lens damage, low IOP.
Multiple FBs with power tools/explosions.
Full-thickness corneal FB → operating room.
Conjunctival FB: irrigate or remove with anaesthetic-soaked swab; buried inert ones can stay.
Conjunctival lac suture: 8-0 Vicryl or 6-0 plain gut; don't bury Tenon's, don't stitch plica/caruncle.
Seidel test; examine fundus under the laceration.
chunks.hook: Hammer + metal = scan for the bit inside.

cards.q: Imaging to exclude intraocular metal fragment?
cards.a: CT orbits (thin cuts); avoid MRI.

cards.q: When to suture a conjunctival laceration?
cards.a: Large ones (≥1–1.5 cm); most heal alone after scleral injury is excluded.

chunks.title: Traumatic iritis & irido/cyclodialysis
chunks.tldr: Traumatic iritis: ache + photophobia 1–3 days after blunt injury; cells/flare; IOP up or down. Rx: cycloplegic ± steroid; at 1 month gonioscopy + scleral depression. Iridodialysis: iris off the spur → diplopia/glare. Cyclodialysis: ciliary body off spur → hypotony, later IOP spike when it closes.
points: Consensual photophobia (light in other eye hurts).
Pupil may be small (spasm) or big (sphincter tears).
Iridodialysis Rx: sunglasses, artificial-pupil CL, repair.
Glaucoma: aqueous suppressants first; avoid miotics (reopen cleft → hypotony).
Cyclodialysis hypotony: atropine + steroids first.
Fellow eye: ~50% risk of open-angle glaucoma in angle-cleavage injuries → watch both eyes.
chunks.hook: Cyclodialysis = soft eye now, hard eye when it shuts.

cards.q: First-line treatment of hypotony from a cyclodialysis cleft?
cards.a: Atropine (to appose ciliary body to sclera) plus steroids.

cards.q: When should gonioscopy be done after blunt trauma?
cards.a: About 1 month after injury (look for angle recession).

chunks.title: Hyphaema: workup & basic care
chunks.tldr: Rule out ruptured globe, measure height, IOP, dilated fundus without depression. Screen for sickle cell. Care: head up, rigid shield (no patch), cycloplegic, no aspirin/NSAIDs, paracetamol, steroid if iritis/fibrin. Rebleed usually day 2–7.
points: 8-ball hyphaema = black, deoxygenated total clot.
Ask: anticoagulants, bleeding history, sickle cell, recent surgery.
Avoid gonioscopy early; UBM/B-scan if view poor; CT if fracture/IOFB/LOC.
Admit: noncompliant, bleeding disorder, other big injuries, sickle + high IOP, young children/amblyopia age, suspected abuse.
Hemolysis (bright red fluid) ≠ rebleed (new bright clot).
Antifibrinolytics (aminocaproic, tranexamic) rarely used now — controversial.
Daily review early; 4 weeks: gonioscopy + depressed fundus exam; possibly yearly for angle recession.
chunks.hook: Shield, sit up, sickle screen, no aspirin.

cards.q: Why a shield not a patch for hyphaema?
cards.a: A patch hides sudden vision change from a rebleed; a rigid shield protects without masking it.

cards.q: When do hyphaema rebleeds usually occur?
cards.a: Days 2–7 after injury.

chunks.title: Hyphaema: IOP & surgery thresholds
chunks.tldr: Non-sickle IOP ≥30: beta-blocker → add alpha-agonist/CAI → oral acetazolamide/mannitol. Sickle: act at ≥24; beta-blocker; avoid topical CAIs, diuretics, alpha-agonists (sickling); methazolamide if needed. Washout if: blood staining, IOP ≥60 × 48 h, ≥25 × 5 days with total hyphaema, not ≤50% by day 8, sickle ≥24 × 24 h.
points: Avoid prostaglandins and miotics (inflammation).
No alpha-agonists in children <2.
If mannitol needed → surgery likely soon.
AC paracentesis = temporising.
Kids at amblyopia risk → consider earlier surgery.
Microhyphaema: suspended RBCs; outpatient; review day 3 and 1 week (daily × 3 if IOP high).
Spontaneous hyphaema: occult trauma/abuse, NVI, clotting disorders, IOL chafing (UGH), HSV, Fuchs, JXG, tumours → gonioscopy, clotting screen, UBM.
chunks.hook: Sickle eyes can't take pressure: treat at 24.

cards.q: Why avoid acetazolamide/dorzolamide in sickle cell hyphaema?
cards.a: Acidosis/low aqueous pH promotes sickling; use beta-blocker, methazolamide only if needed.

cards.q: Name two indications to wash out a hyphaema.
cards.a: Corneal blood staining; IOP ≥60 for 48 h despite therapy (also total hyphaema with IOP ≥25 × 5 days, sickle IOP ≥24 × 24 h, not clearing to 50% by day 8).

chunks.title: Lid laceration: workup & where to repair
chunks.tldr: Check globe, optic nerve, brain first. Laceration nasal to punctum → probe/irrigate canaliculus; dog bites in kids — always probe. Visible fat = septum breached → CT. OR repair if: globe/deep injury, canalicular (can wait up to 4 days), levator, fat, medial canthal avulsion, >⅓ tissue loss.
points: CT if penetrating/severe blunt trauma or LOC.
Glancing blow to zygoma can avulse the medial canthus + canaliculus (looks normal at rest).
Tetanus; antibiotics if contaminated (co-amoxiclav etc.); bites: penicillin, rabies, report.
Bedside: shell over the eye, povidone-iodine 10% (not soap), minimal local/field block.
Don't pull out penetrating FBs in the orbit — imaging + team.
Bites: eyelids' blood supply allows primary repair.
chunks.hook: Fat in the wound = deeper than you think.

cards.q: What does orbital fat in an eyelid wound imply?
cards.a: The orbital septum is breached – needs CT and assessment of levator/EOMs.

cards.q: How urgent is canalicular laceration repair?
cards.a: Not an emergency – can be delayed up to ~4 days.

chunks.title: Lid margin repair technique
chunks.tldr: Key step = realign the tarsus along its whole height (partial-thickness 5-0/6-0 Vicryl) — otherwise notching. Grey-line 6-0 silk 2 mm from edges (alignment only), tie tarsal sutures, then margin, then skin 6-0 plain gut catching the margin suture tails away from cornea.
points: Non-margin: interrupted 6-0 plain/chromic gut; never suture the septum; avoid deep sutures between tarsus and rim.
Tarsal heights: upper ~10 mm (3 sutures), lower ~5 mm (2).
Upper lid tarsal bites lamellar → don't scratch the cornea.
Unreliable/kids: all absorbable (6-0 Vicryl).
Posterior margin suture often unnecessary.
Remove margin sutures 5–10 days, skin 4–7 days; small notch often softens over 3–6 months.
chunks.hook: Fix the tarsus, not just the edge.

cards.q: Most important structural step in marginal lid laceration repair?
cards.a: Reapproximating the tarsus along its full vertical length with lamellar sutures.

chunks.title: Orbital blowout fracture
chunks.tldr: Diplopia, infraorbital numbness, crepitus after nose-blowing, enophthalmos, restricted upgaze. CT orbit + midface (coronal/sagittal, bone windows). Advise no nose blowing, decongestant ×3 days, ice, head up; antibiotics optional. WEBOF (kids): quiet eye + vertical restriction + oculocardiac reflex → repair within 24–48 h.
points: DDx: oedema (improves 7–10 days), nerve palsy (forced ductions free), muscle laceration.
Rule out globe and optic nerve injury first (check pupils, colour).
Eye exam within 48 h for all fractures.
Steroid pack if swelling blocks assessment (not with TBI).
Neurosurgery for roof/frontal sinus/cribriform/intracranial bleed.
Repair 1–2 weeks: persistent primary/downgaze diplopia, >50% floor, early dystopia, complex rim/zygoma/Le Fort.
Delay repair 10–14 days if hyphaema; never with open globe.
Tripod fracture: trismus, malar flattening, rim step.
chunks.hook: Child, white quiet eye, vomiting, can't look up = trapdoor → OR today.

cards.q: Indication for repair of an orbital fracture within 24–48 h?
cards.a: Muscle entrapment with oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope) – typically WEBOF in children.

cards.q: Why avoid nose blowing after orbital fracture?
cards.a: Air forced into the orbit can cause compartment syndrome/optic neuropathy.

chunks.title: Retrobulbar haemorrhage & canthotomy
chunks.tldr: Rock-hard lids, proptosis, RAPD, high IOP after trauma/surgery/anticoagulation = orbital compartment syndrome. Clinical diagnosis — don't wait for CT. Retina dies ~90 min. Do lateral canthotomy + inferior cantholysis with blunt scissors + toothed forceps; lid should fall away from globe.
points: DDx: orbital cellulitis/abscess, tension pneumo-orbit, c-c fistula, varix, lymphangioma (kids).
Canthotomy alone is not enough — must cut the inferior crus (by feel, scissors toward nose).
Success: lid margin moves medially to limbus, IOP falls, retina reperfuses within ~15 min.
Superior cantholysis rarely needed (bleeds from lacrimal gland).
No optic neuropathy but IOP ≥35: stepwise IOP drops.
IV mannitol only to bridge until cantholysis.
Observe 4–6 h if no OCS yet; 12–24 h after decompression (rebleed).
CT 'teardrop/tenting' sign = ominous.
chunks.hook: Hard lids + RAPD = cut now, scan later.

cards.q: Sign of an adequate inferior cantholysis?
cards.a: The lower lid releases from the globe; its lateral margin moves medially to the temporal limbus and IOP drops.

cards.q: Should CT precede canthotomy in suspected orbital compartment syndrome?
cards.a: No – it is a clinical diagnosis; decompress first.

chunks.title: Traumatic optic neuropathy
chunks.tldr: New RAPD after trauma not explained by eye findings. Types: compressive (orbital bleed — commonest), FB, bony canal impingement, sheath haematoma, deceleration (posterior indirect TON). Disc normal early (pallor at once = old disease). Mostly observe; no high-dose steroids with TBI or >8 h (CRASH).
points: Bilateral symmetric TON may show no RAPD — check both eyes in sedated patients.
Colour/red desaturation, confrontation fields.
CT thin cuts through canal; normal CT doesn't exclude TON.
B-scan if avulsion suspected behind haemorrhage.
Sheath haematoma: retinal vein/artery occlusions; consider fenestration if worsening.
Avulsion/laceration: no treatment.
Steroid regimen if used: 30 mg/kg load, 5.4 mg/kg q6h × 48 h + PPI.
Canal decompression only selected progressive cases (dangerous); EPO/TES unproven.
chunks.hook: Forehead hits steering wheel + RAPD + normal eye = indirect TON.

cards.q: Most common type of traumatic optic neuropathy?
cards.a: Compressive optic neuropathy from orbital haemorrhage.

cards.q: When must steroids not be given for TON?
cards.a: With traumatic brain injury or if >8 hours since injury (CRASH).

chunks.title: Intraorbital foreign body
chunks.tldr: Never pull it out at the slit lamp before imaging. CT first (wood can look like air — tell the radiologist; check Hounsfield units). Remove: organic/wood, copper, infection/abscess/fistula, optic nerve compression, large easy-to-reach. Leave: posterior inert metal/glass/stone not compressing anything.
points: Poorly tolerated: wood/vegetable, diesel, pure copper. Fair: brass/bronze. Inert: stone, glass, plastic, iron, lead, steel, aluminium.
≥50% of conjunctival entry wounds are missed — look hard; exclude occult rupture.
MRI only after metal excluded (helps for wood).
B-scan only useful anteriorly.
Globe rupture repaired first.
IV cefazolin for clean inert; organic/dirty → treat as orbital cellulitis.
Wood splinters → repeat surgery, smouldering infection, fibrosis.
Gaze-evoked amaurosis = optic nerve compression.
Posteromedial FB → endonasal approach with ENT.
chunks.hook: Wood is bad and hides as air.

cards.q: Why must wooden orbital foreign bodies be removed?
cards.a: High risk of infection and chronic inflammation; often appear as air on CT.

cards.q: Which inert orbital FBs are usually left?
cards.a: Posterior inorganic ones (glass, stone, steel, lead) not compressing the optic nerve.

chunks.title: Corneal laceration: partial vs full thickness
chunks.tldr: Seidel test decides. Partial thickness: cycloplegic + antibiotic; suture in OR if gaping. Full thickness = open globe (3.14); tiny self-sealed leaks with formed AC: aqueous suppressants, bandage CL, fluoroquinolone, no steroids. Don't measure IOP if Seidel positive.
points: Compare AC depth with fellow eye; shallow = leak.
Iris TIDs or lens damage = the globe is open.
Peripheral lacerations: check they don't extend past limbus.
Deep inert corneal FBs may stay if quiet.
Tetanus for dirty wounds.
chunks.hook: Green river (Seidel +) = hole through.

cards.q: Positive Seidel test means?
cards.a: Aqueous is leaking through a full-thickness wound.

chunks.title: Ruptured globe: what to do
chunks.tldr: Signs: 360° bullous subconj haemorrhage, AC too deep/shallow, peaked pupil, TIDs, lens/vitreous in AC, low IOP, motility limited toward rupture. Then stop examining: shield (no patch), CT, NPO, bed rest, IV antibiotics within 6 h (cefazolin/vanco + moxifloxacin; kids cefazolin + gentamicin), tetanus, antiemetic, analgesia, OR ASAP.
points: B-scan only by ophthalmologist and not with obvious anterior rupture.
Postop: 1 week oral levofloxacin.
Hopeless eye: discuss enucleation early, do it within 7–14 days (sympathetic ophthalmia).
Infection risk ↑: dirty wound, IOFB, broken lens capsule, delayed repair → consider intravitreal antibiotics.
Ocular Trauma Score: start from vision (NLP 60 … ≥20/40 100), minus rupture 23, endophthalmitis 17, perforation 14, RD 11, RAPD 10.
chunks.hook: Shield, scan, starve, shoot antibiotics, stop vomiting.

cards.q: Timing of systemic antibiotics for open globe?
cards.a: Within 6 hours of injury.

cards.q: Why give antiemetics before repair?
cards.a: Vomiting/Valsalva may expel intraocular contents.

chunks.title: Intraocular foreign body
chunks.tldr: Clues: entry wound, iris hole, focal lens opacity, peripheral microcystic corneal oedema (FB hiding in angle). CT thin cuts (no MRI). Severe reaction: iron, steel, copper, vegetable. Inert: glass, gold, lead, stone. Rx: admit NPO, shield, IV vanco + ceftazidime/quinolone, urgent removal (copper/dirty most urgent).
points: Long-standing iron → siderosis: heterochromia, anisocoria, anterior subcapsular cataract, retinopathy, optic atrophy.
BBs/pellets = mostly lead + some iron.
Intraocular air can mimic FB on B-scan; UBM for angle/sulcus FB.
Is it magnetic? Ask what it came from.
Atropine for posterior FBs.
Quinolones avoided in kids/pregnancy.
Retained FB → serial ERG (toxicity often reverses after removal).
chunks.hook: Iron rusts the eye; copper inflames it.

cards.q: Clue to a foreign body hidden in the angle?
cards.a: Sectoral peripheral microcystic corneal oedema.

cards.q: How do you monitor a retained iron IOFB?
cards.a: Serial ERGs for toxic (siderotic) retinopathy.

chunks.title: Fireworks & shrapnel
chunks.tldr: Mix of multiple irregular FBs + burns + chemical + blunt + open globe. Check pH, optic nerve, orbit (where did the fragment stop?), lacrimal system, hearing. Dilate with cycloplegic only if chemical (no phenylephrine). CT; no MRI if metal.
points: Don't dilate if FB lodged in iris.
Inert fragments near vital structures may be left (surgery risks).
Burns → medicine/dermatology/burn unit; facial fractures → ENT/maxfax/neurosurgery.
chunks.hook: Fireworks = burn + blast + bits.

cards.q: Dilating drop to avoid in a firework injury with chemical burn?
cards.a: Phenylephrine (worsens limbal ischaemia).

chunks.title: Commotio, choroidal rupture & sclopetaria
chunks.tldr: Commotio (Berlin oedema): white retina, vessels normal, ± cherry spot; OCT ellipsoid disruption; self-limited. Choroidal rupture: crescent concentric to disc, often hidden by blood at first; watch for CNV (anti-VEGF). Sclopetaria: high-velocity missile passes beside the globe → claw-like chorioretinal rupture, bare sclera.
points: Commotio DDx: RD, artery occlusion, WWOP, myelinated fibres.
Commotio: repeat exam 1–2 weeks; fovea involved may leave RPE scarring.
Rupture DDx: lacquer cracks, angioid streaks.
Long/near-fovea ruptures → higher CNV risk; Amsler grid; review 6–12 monthly.
Sclopetaria: rule out open globe/FB; may have vitreous base avulsion → dialysis; review every 2–4 weeks.
chunks.hook: Sclopetaria = bullet whizzed past and tore the back wall.

cards.q: Late complication of traumatic choroidal rupture?
cards.a: Choroidal neovascularization.

cards.q: What is chorioretinitis sclopetaria?
cards.a: Choroid and retina ruptured by shock wave from a high-velocity missile passing near (not through) the globe.

chunks.title: Purtscher retinopathy
chunks.tldr: Head/chest compression or long-bone fracture (not eye injury) → bilateral peripapillary cotton wool spots, haemorrhages, Purtscher flecken (whitening with clear zone along vessels). Same picture without trauma = pseudo-Purtscher: pancreatitis, malignant HTN, TTP/HUS, lupus, renal failure, amniotic fluid embolism.
points: Mechanism: arteriolar occlusion by complement, fibrin, leukocyte aggregates, fat.
FA: patchy capillary non-perfusion.
No trauma → BP, U&E, FBC, amylase/lipase, rheumatology.
No eye treatment; ~50% regain baseline vision.
chunks.hook: Crushed chest, white spots round the disc.

cards.q: Non-traumatic cause of Purtscher-like retinopathy?
cards.a: Acute pancreatitis (also TTP/HUS, malignant hypertension, lupus).

chunks.title: Shaken baby syndrome
chunks.tldr: Usually <1 yr: irritability, seizures, poor feeding; story doesn't fit. Retinal haemorrhages in ~85%; ⅔ too many to count, multilayered, out to the ora; haemorrhagic macular retinoschisis ± paramacular folds. Brain: subdural haemorrhage. External signs often absent.
points: Asymmetric in up to 20%; unilateral ~2%.
Repeated acceleration–deceleration ± impact.
Document carefully (photos), involve child-protection/paediatrics.
chunks.hook: Too many, too deep, too far = abuse.

cards.q: Pathognomonic-ish macular sign in abusive head trauma?
cards.a: Haemorrhagic macular retinoschisis with perimacular folds.
